title: Claude Certified Associate: practice questions
note: Original practice questions written for this site from Anthropic's Claude Certified Associate – Foundations exam guide (version 1.0, July 2026) and checked against Anthropic's documentation and help center. Not official Anthropic exam material.

exam.differences: The real exam has 60 questions in 120 minutes and passes at a scaled 720 out of 1,000. A full practice exam here is 60 questions too, drawn from 146 and weighted like the real exam.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator types 'Write something about our product launch' and gets a generic result. She needs a usable draft for Friday's customer announcement. Which rewrite is most likely to help?
options: Repeat the request in capital letters so Claude treats it as urgent.
Add the word 'professional' and ask Claude to try again.
State the audience, format, length and key points to include.
Ask Claude to guess the missing details and write the final piece.
questions.explanation: Claude responds best to explicit instructions about the output, its format and its constraints. A vague request forces it to guess.
whyWrong: Capital letters add emphasis but no information about what is wanted.
One vague adjective supplies no audience, format or constraints, so a retry repeats the guess.
Guessing leaves you with a draft built on assumptions you never checked.

questions.stem: An HR specialist tells Claude 'Keep every policy summary under 100 words.' The summaries come out clipped and drop key dates, though staff read them on phones. What change best helps Claude serve the real goal?
options: Explain the purpose: staff read these on phones and need dates.
Lower the limit to 50 words so every word is chosen carefully.
Remove the word limit and let Claude pick a suitable length.
Add a second rule that nothing important may ever be left out.
questions.explanation: Giving the reason or audience behind an instruction lets Claude tailor the answer to your goal rather than follow a bare rule mechanically.
whyWrong: A tighter limit makes losing dates more likely and still says nothing about why brevity matters.
Dropping the limit discards a real requirement instead of explaining it.
Two conflicting rules with no stated purpose leave Claude guessing which one wins.

questions.stem: A project manager's status updates keep arriving as bullet lists. She tried 'Do not use bullet points' and still gets them, but she wants flowing prose for her weekly email. Which revision fits good prompting practice?
options: Repeat 'no bullet points' three times in bold at the end.
Ask for a much longer update to crowd out the bullet lists.
Write the prompt as a bulleted checklist of formats to avoid.
Request flowing paragraphs and write the prompt itself in prose.
questions.explanation: Telling Claude what to do works better than listing what to avoid, and a prompt written in the style you want back nudges the reply toward that style.
whyWrong: Repeating a negative instruction still describes what not to do and leaves the prompt's own style unchanged.
Length does not control formatting, and a longer reply can be just as bulleted.
A bulleted prompt pushes the reply toward bullets, the opposite of the goal.

questions.stem: An operations lead asks Claude in one message to research three vendors, compare pricing, draft a memo and write a rollout plan. The result is shallow. What is the best next step?
options: Resend the same message and ask for a much longer response.
Split it into separate requests: research, comparison, memo, then plan.
Keep one message and tell Claude to try harder on each part.
Switch to the most powerful model and resend the identical message.
questions.explanation: Splitting a sprawling request into substeps lets Claude handle each part well and lets you check the result at each stage.
whyWrong: A longer reply to the same overloaded request spreads the shallowness over more words.
Urging more effort does not fix a request that bundles too many separate jobs.
A different model does not remove the problem of an unstructured, oversized request.

questions.stem: A communications specialist is preparing a customer announcement and wants to catch problems before it goes out. Which two steps follow a prompt-chaining approach? (Choose two.)
options: Paste the draft request, review rubric and polish request into one prompt.
Ask Claude to draft the announcement, then send a separate review prompt.
Start a fresh chat for each stage without carrying earlier output forward.
Read the review yourself before asking Claude to refine the draft.
Have Claude refine the draft immediately and show only the final version.
questions.explanation: Chaining runs draft, review and refine as a sequence where each output feeds the next, which lets you inspect each stage before continuing.
whyWrong: One combined prompt is not a chain and gives you no chance to inspect intermediate results.
Dropping the earlier output breaks the chain, as each stage depends on the one before it.
Hiding the intermediate steps removes the checkpoints that make chaining useful.

questions.stem: A project coordinator is about to ask Claude for a stakeholder update. The readers are senior executives frustrated by project delays, and she wants the right tone on the first try. What should she include in her prompt?
options: Explain who the readers are, how they feel, and the tone needed.
Ask for a 'professional' tone and leave everything else to Claude.
Send a bare request first, then fix the tone through follow-ups.
Add a closing line asking Claude to double-check its tone is suitable.
questions.explanation: Context about the readers and their situation, plus the tone you want, gives Claude what it needs to target the draft on the first try, which cuts down on follow-up rounds.
whyWrong: A generic label like 'professional' says nothing about who the readers are or how they feel.
Follow-ups can refine a draft, but the goal here is the right tone from the start.
A tone self-check cannot succeed when Claude was never told the audience or the feeling to strike.

questions.stem: A support lead wants Claude's reply drafts to match the team's tone and layout. Written descriptions of the style have not worked. What is the best improvement?
options: Include one perfect sample reply and ask Claude to copy it.
Paste thirty near-identical refund replies so the pattern is unmistakable.
Include three to five varied past replies, wrapped in labelled tags.
Add a longer paragraph describing the tone in more adjectives.
questions.explanation: A few relevant, varied examples steer format, tone and structure more reliably than description alone, and tags keep them separate from the instructions.
whyWrong: A single example invites Claude to copy its quirks onto ticket types it does not fit.
Near-identical examples teach one pattern and may cause unintended copying.
More description is the approach that already failed, while examples show what words cannot.

questions.stem: A program manager asks Claude for ideas to boost workshop attendance and gets five safe suggestions. She wants a wide, ambitious list for a team brainstorm. Which prompt change suits the task?
options: Ask for exactly five ideas again, each as short as possible.
Ask Claude to pick the single best idea and defend it.
Ask for a very formal tone to encourage more creative ideas.
Ask for as many ideas as possible, going beyond the obvious.
questions.explanation: For brainstorming, say outright that you want more than the minimum, such as as many relevant options as possible and beyond the basics.
whyWrong: Capping the count and shrinking each item works against a wide, ambitious list.
Narrowing to one idea is the opposite of brainstorming broadly.
Formality does not drive creativity.

questions.stem: An analyst asks Claude for a market-sizing answer that will go into a high-stakes report. Which two prompt additions suit a research task? (Choose two.)
options: State the success criteria and verify claims across independent sources.
Ask for one confident headline figure with no sources attached.
Tell Claude to answer from memory in a single quick pass.
Ask Claude not to mention any uncertainty in the findings.
Ask Claude to compare competing explanations and track its confidence level.
questions.explanation: Research prompts work best with stated success criteria and cross-source verification, plus competing hypotheses and confidence tracking that make findings transparent and checkable.
whyWrong: Dropping sources makes the figure impossible to check, which is risky in a high-stakes report.
Skipping verification across sources undermines a research task.
Hiding uncertainty removes exactly the signal a reader needs to judge the findings.

questions.stem: A finance analyst pastes four long vendor contracts into a prompt and wants a comparison of their termination terms. Where should she put the question for the best results?
options: Put the question first so Claude knows the goal before reading.
Place the contracts first and the question after them.
Repeat the question before and after every contract pasted.
Put the question midway, between the second and third contracts.
questions.explanation: For analysis of long documents, put the documents at the top and the question and instructions at the end, which can improve answer quality.
whyWrong: Placing the question before long documents tends to give weaker results.
Repeating the question clutters a long prompt and is not the recommended layout.
A mid-prompt question gets buried between documents instead of following all of them.

questions.stem: A sales manager's prompt for a client proposal keeps producing off-target drafts. Before sending it again, she wants a quick way to judge whether the prompt itself is clear. What should she do?
options: Cut the prompt to under fifty words so nothing stays ambiguous.
Ask Claude to score how clear the prompt is before running it again.
Give it to a coworker new to the task; note any confusion.
Capitalize the key instructions so Claude gives them more weight.
questions.explanation: If a coworker with no background would be confused by the prompt, Claude is likely to be confused too. Handing it to a fresh reader is a quick, reliable clarity test.
whyWrong: Length is not the issue; a short prompt can be just as ambiguous as a long one.
Claude rating its own prompt is not an independent check of what a newcomer would understand.
Capital letters add emphasis but do not add the missing detail that makes a prompt clear.

questions.stem: An analyst pastes meeting notes, a style guide and her request into one long prompt, and Claude sometimes treats lines inside the notes as instructions. What change best prevents this?
options: Wrap the notes, style guide and request in separate descriptive tags.
Repeat the request at the start, middle and end of the notes.
Write the whole request in capital letters to mark it clearly.
Move the style guide into a second chat to avoid confusion.
questions.explanation: Putting each kind of content in its own labeled tag lets Claude tell instructions, context and inputs apart in a mixed prompt, which reduces misreading.
whyWrong: Repeating the request buries it further in the text and does not mark where the notes begin and end.
Capital letters add emphasis but do not separate pasted notes from the instructions.
Splitting the style guide away removes context Claude needs and leaves the notes unmarked.

questions.stem: An operations coordinator needs Claude to clean a customer list, flag duplicates and then draft outreach emails to the remaining contacts. Each step depends on the one before it. How should she write the prompt?
options: List the three tasks in one paragraph and let Claude order them.
Ask only for the outreach emails and let Claude infer the rest.
Describe the goal loosely and ask Claude to choose its own steps.
Number the steps in the order Claude should perform them.
questions.explanation: When order or completeness of steps matters, giving them as a numbered sequence tells Claude exactly what to do and in what order.
whyWrong: A single paragraph leaves the order and completeness to Claude's guess.
Skipping the cleaning and duplicate steps means they may never be done before the emails go out.
A loose goal leaves Claude free to skip or reorder steps that depend on each other.

questions.stem: A finance associate wants Claude's explanations of lease accounting to sound like an experienced controller advising a manager, not a generic summary. What is the simplest effective change to her prompt?
options: Ask Claude to answer in a more professional and formal voice.
Begin by assigning Claude the role of an experienced controller.
Paste a glossary of accounting terms ahead of every question.
Request a longer reply so more of the expertise shows.
questions.explanation: Assigning a role, even in a single sentence, focuses Claude's tone and behavior on the perspective you need.
whyWrong: A formal voice changes the register but not the perspective of a seasoned controller.
A glossary adds terms but does not set the viewpoint or advisory tone she wants.
More length does not change who Claude sounds like; it only adds words.

questions.stem: A consultant must turn a 60-page client report into a two-page executive briefing and wants to catch mistakes early. Which two steps break the task down well? (Choose two.)
options: Ask first for a list of the report's main findings.
Request the full briefing, charts and speaker notes in one message.
Ask Claude to work silently and show only the final briefing.
Check that list, then use it as input for the briefing draft.
Ask for a one-line summary and treat it as the finished briefing.
questions.explanation: Splitting the work into stages lets her check the findings before they feed the briefing, so errors are caught early rather than buried in a finished document.
whyWrong: One large request bundles several outputs and hides where any mistake came from.
Showing only the final result removes the chance to check the work along the way.
A one-line summary cannot serve as a two-page briefing and skips the staged review she wants.

questions.stem: A legal operations analyst must extract renewal deadlines from 40 contracts, then draft a calendar summary for partners. A missed deadline would carry into the summary, and her review time is limited. What approach fits best?
options: Request both the extraction and the summary in one prompt, then proofread.
Draft the summary first, then extract deadlines to match it.
Extract deadlines first, check them, then feed them into the summary.
Run both tasks in separate chats and merge the results afterward.
questions.explanation: Running the tasks as a sequence lets her inspect the extraction output before it feeds the summary, so an error is caught at the stage where it starts.
whyWrong: Doing both at once hides extraction errors inside the finished summary, where they are harder to spot.
Writing the summary before the data exists reverses the dependency and invites guesses.
Separate chats break the link between the steps, so the summary may not use the checked deadlines.

questions.stem: An executive assistant wants three-sentence summaries of long email threads, but Claude's replies keep running long even when she asks it to 'keep it tight.' What should she change?
options: Add 'keep it tight' again at the end of every prompt.
Regenerate the reply until a short one happens to appear.
Ask for a long summary and trim it herself each time.
Ask outright for a three-sentence summary with no preamble.
questions.explanation: Claude can default to longer answers, so brevity should be requested explicitly with a concrete length rather than a vague phrase.
whyWrong: 'Keep it tight' is the vague wording that already failed; repeating it adds nothing.
Regenerating is luck rather than a fix, and gives no control over length.
Trimming by hand does the work Claude could do from a clear length instruction.

questions.stem: A customer success manager's first draft of a renewal email is too long and too pushy. She replies 'make it better' twice, and the draft barely changes. What is the best next move?
options: Start a new chat and retype the original prompt unchanged.
Point to the pushy lines and say how to change them.
Ask Claude to guess what she dislikes and fix everything.
Switch to a different Claude model and run the prompt again.
questions.explanation: Iterating works best with specific feedback: say what is wrong and what change you want, so Claude can act on it directly.
whyWrong: Retyping the same prompt in a new chat discards the draft and repeats the same unclear request.
Asking Claude to guess leaves the problem undefined, much like 'make it better.'
A different model does not fix a vague request; the feedback still lacks detail.

questions.stem: A finance analyst pastes a quarterly churn table into Claude and asks only 'thoughts?', receiving generic remarks. Which two additions best suit an analysis task? (Choose two.)
options: Ask for as many wide-ranging ideas as possible beyond the basics.
Request a creative, imaginative voice to surface hidden patterns.
State the decision the analysis supports and the question to answer.
Ask for a longer reply with general background on churn.
Name the comparisons to examine and the output format wanted.
questions.explanation: An analysis task needs a clear purpose and specific measures or comparisons, so Claude can focus on what the decision requires and return it in a usable form.
whyWrong: Asking for many ideas beyond the basics suits brainstorming, not focused analysis of a table.
An imaginative voice invites invention rather than disciplined reading of the data.
General background adds length but does not point Claude at the question she needs answered.

questions.stem: A product lead needs a wide range of campaign ideas, then a choice among them under a fixed budget. She wants ambitious options without losing a disciplined final pick. Which approach fits?
options: Brainstorm broadly first, then rank the ideas against budget criteria.
Ask for the three best ideas that fit the budget outright.
Request one list of safe ideas, already sorted by likely cost.
Ask for a single idea, then iterate on it until it fits.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming and selecting are different task types. Asking for breadth first, then ranking against stated criteria, serves both goals.
whyWrong: Filtering to the budget up front cuts off the wide, ambitious range she wants.
Asking for safe, pre-sorted ideas works against the ambitious brainstorm she needs.
Starting from one idea gives no range to choose from, so the ranking step never happens.

questions.stem: A communications lead asks Claude to draft a case study from her interview notes. The draft includes a striking customer quotation she does not remember seeing in the notes. What should she do before publishing?
options: Keep the quotation if the wording sounds like the customer's voice.
Ask Claude to confirm the quotation is accurate before publishing.
Search the notes and recording for it; cut it if missing.
Shorten the quotation so any inaccuracy is less noticeable to readers.
questions.explanation: Claude can produce quotations that sound authoritative but have no basis in the source, so quoted wording must be matched against the original material before use.
whyWrong: Claude can invent plausible quotations, and fitting the customer's voice is not evidence they said it.
Claude agreeing with itself is not an independent check; the original source is.
Shortening hides the problem rather than checking whether the customer said it.

questions.stem: An operations analyst receives a vendor comparison from Claude that is well organized and written with total assurance. A teammate says the polish shows it is reliable. How should the analyst treat it?
options: Spot-check the key figures and claims against the vendors' own documents.
Accept it and trust that errors usually look messy.
Accept it and treat the confident tone as strong evidence.
Ask Claude to rewrite it more cautiously, then rely on that version.
questions.explanation: Claude's mistakes can read as polished and plausible, so fluent, confident writing is not evidence of accuracy; key facts need checking against sources.
whyWrong: Errors can look polished and plausible; messy formatting is not a signal of mistakes.
Tone does not reflect how well supported the content is.
A softer tone changes the wording, not whether the figures are correct.

questions.stem: A project manager uses Claude with web search to summarize a regulator's guidance for her team. The summary cites three pages, and she plans to forward it as the team's reference. What should she do first?
options: Forward it, treating the three citations as proof of accuracy.
Ask Claude to add more citations before she forwards it.
Ask Claude whether it is sure, then forward it if yes.
Open the cited pages and compare them with the summary.
questions.explanation: Citations let you verify, but a summary can leave out context that changes a source's meaning, so opening the cited pages is the check that matters.
whyWrong: Citations make checking possible; they do not guarantee nothing was lost or misread.
More citations do not show that the summary matches what the pages say.
Claude's own assurance is not an independent check against the source pages.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator asks Claude, without web search, for the current subscription prices of three competitors and what each launched this quarter. The answer is going into a planning deck. What is the best approach?
options: Use the answer as given, trusting Claude's wide training on public pricing.
Check prices and launches against the competitors' current websites before use.
Ask Claude to restate the prices in a table for reliability.
Verify the prices on current sites but keep the launch details.
questions.explanation: Each model has a knowledge cutoff and may not know later events, so prices, dates and recent developments should be verified against current sources.
whyWrong: Training data may be out of date, so prices and launches can have changed after the cutoff.
A table changes presentation, not whether the information is current.
Launch details are just as time-sensitive as prices and can also be outdated.

questions.stem: A procurement specialist uploads a 60-page supplier contract. She wants Claude's risk analysis to be traceable to the contract text, with fewer made-up details. Which prompt approach fits best?
options: Ask Claude to answer confidently so the analysis reads as decisive.
Run the request several times and keep the longest answer.
Have Claude pull word-for-word quotes first, then analyze using only those.
Tell Claude to write in short, plain sentences.
questions.explanation: For long documents, extracting exact quotes first and basing the analysis only on them grounds the answer in the text and makes each point traceable.
whyWrong: Asking for confidence does not ground answers and can encourage unsupported claims.
Comparing runs can reveal inconsistencies, but keeping the longest answer is not grounding.
Sentence style does not tie conclusions to the actual contract wording.

questions.stem: An analyst has Claude summarize a pasted market report for a leadership update. The report may not cover every question she asks, and she wants fewer invented details. Which two prompt instructions help most? (Choose two.)
options: Tell Claude never to leave any question unanswered in the summary.
Allow Claude to say it lacks information when the report is silent.
Ask Claude to rate each claim and trust anything scoring 8 or higher.
Ask for a supporting quote per claim and drop any without one.
Ask Claude to write in a more formal, authoritative register.
questions.explanation: Giving Claude explicit permission to admit missing information, and having it back each claim with a quote and drop unsupported ones, both reduce fabricated content.
whyWrong: Forcing an answer to every question pushes Claude to fill gaps with invented content.
Self-rated scores are not a reliable accuracy signal, so they cannot filter out made-up claims.
Formality changes style and can make unsupported claims sound more convincing.

questions.stem: A finance associate asks Claude the same question about a figure in a long report three times. Two answers give one growth rate and the third gives a different one. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Check the figure against the report itself before using any answer.
Add the word 'accurate' to the prompt to force consistency.
Accept the longest answer, which includes the most detail.
Go with the two matching answers and ignore the odd one.
questions.explanation: Inconsistencies between repeated runs of the same prompt can signal a hallucination, so the figure should be confirmed against the source document.
whyWrong: A single word does not make answers consistent or verified.
Length is not a measure of correctness; detail can be invented too.
Even a majority can be wrong, so the figure still has to be checked in the source.

questions.stem: A policy writer wants to see whether Claude treats both sides of a contested workplace issue fairly in a briefing. She has time for only one kind of check. Which check is most useful?
options: Ask Claude whether it believes it was biased, then trust its answer.
Send the request from each opposing viewpoint and compare the answers.
Run the request once and judge whether the tone feels neutral.
Swap the topic for a less sensitive one and compare the answers.
questions.explanation: Sending the same contested request from opposing viewpoints and comparing depth, counterarguments and refusals is a practical way to spot uneven treatment.
whyWrong: Self-assessment is not evidence of balance; comparing actual responses is.
A single run judged by feel can miss uneven depth or hidden refusals.
Changing the topic stops testing the contested issue she cares about.

questions.stem: A team runs one pair of mirrored prompts on a sensitive social topic and finds the answers look balanced. They plan to publish Claude's draft with no further review. What is the best judgment?
options: Publish, treating one balanced pair as proof the draft is unbiased.
Publish, treating the absence of refusals as proof of neutrality.
Rerun the pair until it looks balanced, then publish.
Have a person review the draft before it goes out.
questions.explanation: Bias checks are imperfect, there is no agreed definition of bias, and results can differ from run to run, so sensitive content still needs human review.
whyWrong: One result cannot prove anything when outputs vary between runs.
Not refusing is only one dimension; depth and counterarguments matter too.
Rerunning until it looks balanced selects the result you hoped for rather than testing it.

questions.stem: A compliance coordinator used careful prompting, including permission to say 'I don't know' and requests for supporting quotes, to produce a summary for a client notice. The summary looks clean. What is the right next step?
options: Send it, trusting that careful prompting removes hallucinations in practice.
Send it without review, given that the notice is short.
Have someone qualified validate the critical facts before sending.
Ask Claude to add a note saying the compliance team verified it.
questions.explanation: Prompting techniques reduce hallucinations but do not eliminate them, so critical facts in high-stakes material still need independent validation.
whyWrong: These techniques lower the risk but never remove it entirely.
Quotes help, yet they can still be misread or misapplied, and a client notice calls for review.
A note claiming verification does not make it true and misleads the client.

questions.stem: A project lead has a two-page project brief in a document artifact. Only the second paragraph reads too technical for the executives receiving it. What is the most efficient way to fix it?
options: Ask Claude to regenerate the whole brief in an executive tone.
Start a new chat and paste the brief to revise it again.
Highlight that paragraph and use Edit with Claude to simplify it.
Copy the brief to a word processor and rewrite it by hand.
questions.explanation: In a document artifact you can highlight a passage and use Edit with Claude so only that section is revised and the rest stays unchanged.
whyWrong: Regenerating everything may alter parts that were already fine.
A new chat discards the existing artifact context and is unnecessary for one paragraph.
Rewriting by hand skips a built-in feature that does the targeted edit for her.

questions.stem: An HR specialist has a staff newsletter artifact she likes. She wants to try a much more casual direction and compare it with the current version without losing it. What should she do?
options: Edit an earlier message to branch the chat, keeping the original artifact.
Overwrite the artifact with the casual version and recreate the first later.
Ask Claude to merge both tones into one newsletter.
Delete the chat so Claude starts over with fresh tone instructions.
questions.explanation: Editing an earlier message creates a separate branch with its own artifacts, so she can explore a new direction and keep the earlier version.
whyWrong: Overwriting risks losing the version she likes, and branching avoids that.
Merging the tones produces a third version and does not let her compare the two.
Deleting the chat removes the work she wants to compare against.

questions.stem: An operations lead asks Claude to create a Word report from a data spreadsheet for a client meeting. The first file is close but not exactly what she needs. Which two actions best fit good practice? (Choose two.)
options: Describe the structure, content and formatting wanted in the next request.
Send the file as-is, trusting that generated files reflect the data exactly.
Check the file's content against her spreadsheet data before sharing it.
Ask Claude to shrink the file size to improve accuracy.
Switch to PDF so the report no longer needs review.
questions.explanation: Generated files may not meet exact requirements on the first try, so state the structure, content and formatting you want and check the result before sharing.
whyWrong: Files can miss requirements or contain errors, so sending without review is risky.
File size has no bearing on whether the content is accurate.
The file format does not remove the need to review the content.

questions.stem: A finance associate wants Claude to turn a list of monthly expenses into a budget tracker that recalculates totals and shows a chart when numbers change. Which output type fits best?
options: A PowerPoint deck with the totals and chart on slides.
An Excel spreadsheet with working formulas and a built-in chart.
A Word report that describes the totals in prose.
A table in the chat that she retypes each month.
questions.explanation: Excel files can hold working formulas and charts, which suits a tracker that must recalculate when the numbers change.
whyWrong: A deck presents results but will not recalculate when the data changes.
A Word report suits analysis with commentary, not a live calculating tracker.
A chat table cannot recalculate and relies on error-prone manual retyping.

questions.stem: A team lead makes several requests in one chat and wants anything she will edit, reuse or share kept as a standalone document. Which two outputs would Claude most likely place in an artifact? (Choose two.)
options: A 40-line onboarding checklist she will edit and reuse next quarter
A conversational explanation of why last quarter's launch slipped, for her own understanding
A self-contained one-page FAQ she plans to share with new hires
A quick definition of one term she asked about in passing
A yes-or-no answer about a calendar conflict
questions.explanation: Claude uses artifacts for substantial, self-contained content, typically over about 15 lines, that you will edit, reuse or share; short or conversational answers stay inline.
whyWrong: A conversational explanation is long but is read once in the chat, so it stays inline.
A short definition is a brief snippet that stays inline.
A quick yes-or-no is a short answer and stays inline.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst asks Claude for a market-size estimate, and Claude adds that it is 95% sure of the figure. The number will anchor a board slide. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Accept the figure and cite Claude's stated confidence in the slide notes.
Ask Claude to rate its confidence again and use the average.
Verify the figure against an independent, reliable source first.
Label the number as approximate on the slide and move on.
questions.explanation: Models judge their own answers imperfectly, especially on unfamiliar tasks, so a stated confidence level is not proof. A figure that anchors a board slide needs an independent check.
whyWrong: Stated confidence is not evidence of accuracy, especially on unfamiliar tasks.
A second self-rating comes from the same source and adds no independent check.
A label does not make an unchecked number reliable for a board decision.

questions.stem: A team member catches Claude giving a confident but wrong answer about an internal process. Besides correcting her own notes, which step does Anthropic's help guidance recommend?
options: Use the thumbs-down button to report the response.
Delete the whole conversation and start a fresh one later.
Ask Claude to promise it will not repeat the mistake.
Switch to a different model and drop the original chat.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's help article on incorrect responses points users to the thumbs-down button for reporting a bad answer, alongside checking important claims themselves.
whyWrong: Deleting the chat neither reports the problem nor improves the product.
A promise inside one chat does not change how the model behaves.
Changing models does not report the problem and may repeat the error.

questions.stem: A policy analyst has Claude summarize a long supplier agreement for her director. The summary reads cleanly. Before she tells the director it is complete, what is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask Claude whether it left anything out and accept its reply.
Forward it, noting that the writing is clear and consistent.
Request a shorter version that keeps only the key points.
Compare the summary with the agreement for omitted terms.
questions.explanation: A summary can drop context that changes the meaning of a source, so completeness is checked by reading the original. Fluent writing is not evidence that nothing is missing.
whyWrong: Claude checking its own summary is not an independent completeness check.
Clear writing says nothing about whether important terms were left out.
Cutting the text further removes more content and makes gaps likelier.

questions.stem: A finance associate gets a margin calculation from Claude that looks off. She wants to see how Claude reasoned so she can spot a faulty assumption. What should she use?
options: Turn on web search so Claude lists the sources it used.
Turn on thinking and read its reasoning summary.
Ask Claude to present the same answer again in a table.
Raise the effort level and accept the answer if it matches.
questions.explanation: The thinking toggle shows an expandable summary of Claude's approach, which lets a reviewer see the reasoning and catch faulty logic or assumptions.
whyWrong: Web search adds sources but does not show how the calculation was reasoned.
A new layout repeats the same result without exposing the reasoning.
A matching result can repeat the same flawed assumption.

questions.stem: A communications specialist has Claude draft a product announcement from three internal briefs. She needs every claim in the draft to be traceable to those briefs. Which follow-up fits best?
options: Ask Claude to rewrite the announcement in a more cautious tone.
Ask Claude to score each claim for likelihood from one to ten.
Ask Claude to quote support for each claim and cut the rest.
Ask Claude to draft the announcement again from scratch.
questions.explanation: Asking Claude to find a supporting quote for every claim, and to remove any it cannot support, makes the draft auditable against the briefs.
whyWrong: A cautious tone does not tie claims to the briefs.
Likelihood scores are self-ratings, not evidence from the briefs.
A fresh draft can introduce new unsupported claims.

questions.stem: A research coordinator uses Claude with web search to prepare a competitor briefing that will inform a leadership decision. Which two steps best validate the answer? (Choose two.)
options: Open the cited pages and confirm they support each statement.
Treat the presence of citations as proof the claims are correct.
Ask Claude to confirm that its own summary is accurate.
Favor authoritative sources for the facts that drive the decision.
Turn web search off and ask the same question again.
questions.explanation: The cited pages can contain context missing from Claude's summary, so they should be opened, and authoritative sources should anchor facts that matter for important decisions.
whyWrong: Citations show where Claude looked, not that the summary represents the pages correctly.
A self-review is not independent of the original answer.
Without search Claude lacks current information and cannot confirm the first answer.

questions.stem: A benefits analyst finds a precise percentage in Claude's draft employee guide, with no source named. She does not recognize it. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep the percentage and ask colleagues whether it sounds right.
Trace the percentage to a primary source, or remove it.
Ask Claude to add a footnote naming a plausible source.
Reword it as 'around' that number so it reads less exact.
questions.explanation: Claude can state specific figures with no basis, so a number is checked against an original source or left out. Reworded or footnoted claims still need real support.
whyWrong: Familiarity is not verification, and colleagues may share the same assumption.
A requested footnote can be invented and gives false assurance.
Softer wording still publishes a number nobody has confirmed.

questions.stem: A sales manager needs a client's announcements from the past two weeks for tomorrow's call. Claude, with no search, names none. How should he proceed?
options: Ask Claude to infer likely announcements from the client's past patterns.
Ask Claude to think longer and answer again without search.
Assume the client made no announcements and plan accordingly.
Use web search, then review the pages Claude cites.
questions.explanation: A model may not know events after its cutoff. Web search suits recent or changing information, and its cited sources should still be reviewed.
whyWrong: Inferred announcements would be guesses presented as findings.
More thinking cannot supply events after the model's knowledge cutoff.
An answer with no search is not evidence that nothing happened.

questions.stem: A contracts coordinator has Claude draft a termination clause for a customer agreement that will be signed next week. Time is short. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Have counsel or another qualified reviewer check it first.
Ask Claude to list the clause's weaknesses and sign if none appear.
Run the same prompt twice and sign if the drafts match.
Add a note that AI helped draft the clause and sign.
questions.explanation: Prompting techniques reduce errors but never remove them, and a signed contract is high stakes, so a qualified person should check the clause first.
whyWrong: Claude reviewing its own draft is not independent human review.
Matching drafts can repeat the same error and are no substitute for review.
A disclosure note does not check the legal content.

questions.stem: An editor will publish a Claude-drafted explainer on a contested policy question. Which two actions best address possible bias? (Choose two.)
options: Run one pair of mirrored prompts and publish if the results match.
Compare Claude's replies to mirrored prompts from opposing viewpoints.
Add a disclaimer that Claude may be biased and publish as written.
Ask Claude whether its own draft is biased and accept the reply.
Have a person read the draft for balance before it goes out.
questions.explanation: Paired prompts from opposing sides let you compare depth, caveats and refusals, and because such checks are imperfect, a person should still review sensitive content.
whyWrong: One passing check is limited, since results vary between runs and bias has no agreed measure.
A disclaimer warns readers but does not check the content.
A self-assessment is not an independent check of balance.

questions.stem: A communications manager has three Claude outputs due today: brainstormed event names, a draft lunch invitation, and a summary of regulatory changes for a client filing. She can verify only one in depth. Which?
options: Check the event-name list for originality and fit.
Check the lunch invitation for tone and correct details.
Check the regulatory summary against the official sources.
Split the time evenly and spot-check each of the three outputs.
questions.explanation: Verification effort should follow the stakes. A regulatory summary feeding a client filing carries the most risk, and it contains facts that can be wrong or out of date.
whyWrong: A weak name idea is easily spotted and low in consequence.
A small error in an invitation is quick to fix and low in consequence.
Even spot-checks leave the high-stakes filing under-verified.

questions.stem: A training manager opens an interactive quiz that Claude built as an artifact and sees an error message. Which built-in option sends the error details back to Claude to repair?
options: Highlight text and choose Edit with Claude.
Click Try fixing with Claude on the error.
Edit an earlier message to branch the chat.
Export the artifact and open it elsewhere.
questions.explanation: When an artifact shows an error, the Try fixing with Claude option sends the error details to Claude, though a fix is not guaranteed.
whyWrong: Edit with Claude revises a highlighted passage in a document and does not target errors.
Branching starts a separate version and does not report the error.
Exporting moves the artifact elsewhere without fixing the error.

questions.stem: A product analyst must send executives a version of a technical findings memo. Claude's first rewrite is still too detailed for them. What is the best next step?
options: Ask Claude to cut the memo down to a fixed number of words.
Start a new chat and paste the memo in again.
Rewrite the memo by hand to save revision time.
Tell Claude who the executives are and their decision.
questions.explanation: Replying in the same chat with the audience and its purpose gives Claude the context to adapt the memo, which is how outputs are refined for a reader.
whyWrong: A word count trims text without fitting it to the readers' needs.
Restarting discards the context already built in the chat.
Hand rewriting skips the quick refinement Claude can do.

questions.stem: A program manager drafted a status report in a document artifact and now must send it to a partner who works in Word. What should she do?
options: Export the document artifact as a Word file.
Copy the text into an email and ask the partner to format it.
Ask Claude to recreate the report as a spreadsheet.
Take screenshots of the artifact and send those.
questions.explanation: Docs artifacts can be exported to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so the report can be sent in the format the partner uses.
whyWrong: Pasting loses the formatting and shifts the work to the partner.
A spreadsheet is the wrong form for a written report.
Screenshots cannot be edited in Word.

questions.stem: A finance lead needs two deliverables for next week's board meeting and plans to use Claude's file creation. Which two format choices fit the task? (Choose two.)
options: A budget model with formulas, as an Excel file.
A quarterly results presentation deck, as a Word document.
A report with charts and commentary, as a Word file.
A recalculating monthly expense tracker, as a PDF file.
A slide presentation for the board, as a PNG image.
questions.explanation: Excel suits models with working formulas, and Word suits reports that combine data, charts and commentary. Slide decks belong in PowerPoint.
whyWrong: A deck belongs in PowerPoint, not Word.
A PDF does not recalculate when numbers change.
A PNG is a single image, not a slide deck.

questions.stem: A support lead wants every customer-call summary in the same fields so the team can paste results into a tracker. Claude's layout keeps varying between calls. Which fix fits best?
options: Ask for a consistent layout in every message you send.
Request longer, more detailed summaries of each call.
Raise the effort level for every call summary.
Give Claude a template listing the exact fields.
questions.explanation: Defining the exact structure you want, such as a template, makes Claude follow every formatting element consistently.
whyWrong: A general request leaves the structure open to interpretation.
More detail adds length without fixing the structure.
More reasoning does not fix a missing structure.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst on a paid plan needs a briefing on how regional competitors price similar services. It needs many sources, plus files in her connected Drive. Which feature fits best?
options: Use a standard chat with web search turned off
Run Research across the web and her Drive
Ask Claude to build an artifact for the briefing
Turn on Memory so Claude recalls earlier pricing chats
questions.explanation: Research runs multiple searches that build on each other, drawing on the web and connected tools, which suits a question needing several sources.
whyWrong: Without searching, the reply cannot draw on current pricing sources or her Drive files.
An artifact holds a finished output; it does not gather sources.
Memory recalls past chat topics and does not research new information.

questions.stem: A consultant produces a monthly client report using the same style guide and data dictionary each time, and wants every month's work organized. Which setup suits this best?
options: Keep extending one very long chat every month
Start a new chat each month and repaste the guide
Save the guide and dictionary in an artifact
Create a project with both files and monthly chats
questions.explanation: A project bundles its own instructions, uploaded knowledge and chat history, so related recurring work stays focused and each chat starts with the same reference material.
whyWrong: A single ever-growing chat will eventually hit the length limit and uses more of the usage limit.
Re-pasting each month is repetitive and error-prone when a project can store the documents once.
Artifacts are outputs saved in a tab; they are not automatically loaded into new chats.

questions.stem: A training manager must send new hires the same onboarding checklist every quarter, edited each time. She wants a feature that makes it easy to refine and find again. What fits best?
options: Make it an artifact she can reopen and refine
Ask for an inline reply and copy it each quarter
Put the checklist text in a project's instruction box
Run Research each quarter to rebuild the checklist
questions.explanation: Artifacts are standalone outputs such as documents that open beside the chat, can be edited, and are saved in an Artifacts tab for reuse.
whyWrong: Inline replies sit inside the conversation and are harder to reuse and find later.
Instructions steer how Claude behaves in a project; they are not a place to store deliverables.
Research is for multi-source investigation, which a simple checklist does not need.

questions.stem: A support team must sort thousands of short ticket subjects into five categories every morning. Speed and cost matter and the reasoning is simple. Which model tier fits best?
options: Opus, the most capable tier, for the best labels
Sonnet with extended reasoning turned on for every ticket
Haiku, the fastest and lowest-cost tier
Whichever model offers the largest context window
questions.explanation: Haiku is the fastest, cheapest tier, built for high-volume, speed-sensitive work such as classification and extraction.
whyWrong: The top tier costs more and runs slower than a simple sorting job needs.
Heavy reasoning on every short ticket spends time and usage on a simple task.
Context window size is not the deciding factor for short, simple, high-volume items.

questions.stem: A communications lead drafts and edits varied materials all day and wants strong writing with quick responses, without paying for the most expensive tier. Which tier is the best match?
options: Sonnet, which balances intelligence, speed and mid-range cost
Haiku, which is the strongest tier at polished writing
Opus, which is the fastest tier for all-day editing
Haiku for drafts and Opus for every edit
questions.explanation: Sonnet is the tier that combines strong intelligence with fast speed, sitting between Haiku and Opus on cost.
whyWrong: Haiku is the fastest and cheapest tier, not the strongest at nuanced writing.
Opus is the more capable tier at moderate speed and higher cost, not the fastest.
One balanced tier can handle both drafting and editing; splitting them adds cost and effort.

questions.stem: A policy advisor must analyze a dozen dense reports over several hours, and quality matters far more than turnaround. Which choice best aligns the model with the task?
options: Haiku, so its low cost allows many repeat runs
Whichever model is selected by default
Opus, the tier built for long knowledge work
Sonnet, the balanced tier, with extended reasoning off
questions.explanation: Opus is the more capable tier, suited to long-running knowledge work where quality matters more than speed, at moderate speed and higher cost.
whyWrong: Haiku is optimized for speed and volume, not for demanding multi-hour analysis.
The tiers differ in capability, speed and cost, so the choice matters.
Sonnet balances speed and cost; the deepest long-running analysis calls for the most capable tier.

questions.stem: A researcher's chat has grown very long and is hitting the length limit, and she is also close to her session usage limit. Which two actions help most? (Choose two.)
options: Start a new chat with the key points
Keep adding to the same chat to save usage
Switch Memory off to clear the current context window
Turn off extended thinking and unneeded connectors
Wait five hours for the length limit to reset
questions.explanation: A length limit is fixed by the context window, so a new chat is the fix, and long chats use more usage. Turning off extended thinking and unneeded connectors also saves usage.
whyWrong: Longer chats use more of the usage limit, not less.
Memory is a separate feature and does not reset a conversation's context window.
The length limit is separate from the usage limit and does not reset on a timer.

questions.stem: A consultant notices Claude has saved an outdated client detail as a memory and keeps mentioning it in new chats. She wants it gone, not ignored. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait for the five-hour session limit to reset first
Delete the topic in Settings > Memory
Add the corrected detail to the project's knowledge base
Start a new chat and expect the memory to vanish
questions.explanation: Memories are listed as topics under Settings > Memory, where individual ones can be deleted, and the page says you can also tell Claude in a chat to forget something.
whyWrong: The session limit is about usage and has no effect on saved memories.
Project knowledge is separate and does not override or delete saved memories.
Memory carries across chats, so a new chat can still use the saved detail.

questions.stem: A field sales rep wants to speak a long prompt into her phone and later scan Claude's reply as written text, without any spoken back-and-forth. Which feature fits best?
options: Voice mode in the mobile app, with Claude replying aloud.
Dictation in the mobile app, which converts speech to text.
Cowork in the mobile app to run the task for her.
Research mode in the mobile app for a written report.
questions.explanation: Dictation turns what you say into typed prompt text and Claude replies in text. Voice mode is a two-way spoken conversation.
whyWrong: Voice mode has Claude speak its responses back, which she does not want.
Cowork carries out multi-step tasks; it does not exist to turn speech into a typed prompt.
Research mode produces a report but is not the feature that converts speech into prompt text.

questions.stem: An operations analyst on a paid plan wants Claude to sort 300 files in a folder on her desktop into subfolders and build a summary spreadsheet. Which feature fits best?
options: Research mode, pointed at the folder's contents.
A new Project with all 300 files uploaded as knowledge.
A single chat that returns an artifact listing the folder.
Cowork on desktop, with the folder connected to Claude.
questions.explanation: Cowork plans and carries out multi-step file tasks, and on desktop it can read and write files in folders you connect, with no manual uploads.
whyWrong: Research mode gathers and cites sources; it does not reorganize files in a folder.
A Project holds reference knowledge for chats; it does not sort files into subfolders for her.
An artifact is an output beside the chat and cannot rearrange files on her desktop.

questions.stem: A recruiter wants Claude to open several job board pages in her browser, read the postings, and click through to each listing for her. Which feature is designed for this?
options: Claude in Chrome, the extension that reads, clicks and navigates sites.
Research mode, which runs linked searches and returns a cited report.
The Drive connector, which retrieves files and extracts their text.
An artifact, which opens beside the chat as a standalone output.
questions.explanation: Claude in Chrome is a browser extension that lets Claude read, click and navigate websites on your behalf.
whyWrong: Research mode searches and reports; it does not click through pages or operate websites.
The Drive connector retrieves files from Drive, not pages in her browser.
An artifact is an output Claude creates; it does not operate websites.

questions.stem: A consultant does not want Claude to draw on her everyday, non-project memories while working inside one confidential client project. What is the most appropriate setting change?
options: Delete each of her everyday memories in Settings > Memory.
Run the project's chats in incognito mode instead.
Turn off 'Use account memory' on that project's page.
Ask Claude in every chat to ignore earlier memories.
questions.explanation: Inside a project, Claude uses that project's memory plus non-project memory. Turning off 'Use account memory' on the project keeps its memory fully separate.
whyWrong: Deleting everyday memories destroys useful history for all her other work.
Incognito chats exist outside projects, so this does not fit work inside the project.
Asking in every chat is easy to forget and does not change what Claude can access.

questions.stem: A department head assumes the most capable Claude tier is always the right choice for her team's work, from quick tagging to deep analysis. Which principle should guide model choice instead?
options: Choose the newest tier available by default, whatever the task is.
Choose the cheapest tier for every task to protect usage limits.
Choose one tier per team so every output stays consistent.
Match the tier to the task, saving heavier ones for hard reasoning.
questions.explanation: Lighter, faster models suit simple high-volume work, while the more capable tiers are worth their cost when the reasoning is demanding.
whyWrong: Defaulting to the newest or biggest tier ignores speed and cost for simple tasks.
The cheapest tier can fall short on demanding analysis, so it is not right for every task.
A single tier for everything wastes capacity on easy work and under-serves hard work.

questions.stem: A team lead is deciding which jobs to hand to Claude's lightest, fastest, lowest-cost tier to save time and usage. Which two tasks suit it best? (Choose two.)
options: Reasoning through the legal implications of a company merger.
Tagging 500 survey responses by sentiment each morning.
Synthesizing a dozen dense reports into a board strategy memo.
Pulling invoice numbers and dates from hundreds of emails.
Cross-checking contradictions across a long set of research papers.
questions.explanation: The lightest tier is built for high-volume, speed-sensitive work such as classification and extraction. Demanding synthesis and reasoning belong with more capable tiers.
whyWrong: Weighing legal implications is demanding reasoning that suits a more capable tier.
A dense, multi-report synthesis is quality-critical work for a more capable tier.
Finding contradictions across many papers is heavy reasoning, not simple high-volume work.

questions.stem: A policy advisor has one multi-hour synthesis of dense reports for a board paper, plus twenty quick reformatting jobs the same day, and her usage budget is limited. How should she match models to the work?
options: Use the most capable tier for all twenty-one jobs.
Use the lightest tier for all jobs to save usage.
Use a stronger tier for the synthesis and a lighter one for reformatting.
Use the capable tier first, then switch to lighter ones once usage runs low.
questions.explanation: Quality matters most for the demanding synthesis, while the routine reformatting does not need a heavy model. Matching each job to a tier balances quality, speed and usage.
whyWrong: Spending the heaviest tier on simple reformatting wastes a limited usage budget.
The lightest tier risks weak quality on the board-level synthesis, where quality matters most.
Switching only when usage runs low is arbitrary and risks hitting the limit before the work is done.

questions.stem: A marketing analyst on a paid plan keeps hitting her session usage limit by midweek. Most of her requests are routine caption reformatting handled by the most capable tier. What should she change?
options: Keep the same model but write much longer prompts.
Switch routine reformatting to a lighter, faster model.
Wait for the weekly reset before sending routine requests.
Turn on automatic context management to expand her usage allowance.
questions.explanation: Choosing a lighter model for routine tasks is a recommended way to stretch usage limits, since model choice affects how fast usage is consumed.
whyWrong: Longer prompts use more of her allowance, not less.
Waiting delays the work instead of fixing the cause of the drain.
Automatic context management keeps long chats going but makes them use more usage, not an expanded allowance.

questions.stem: At the start of a new workday, a Pro user sees a message that her long conversation cannot continue, though she has used little of her usage allowance. What is the best response?
options: Start a new conversation; this is a length limit, not usage.
Wait five hours for the session limit to reset, then resume.
Delete earlier messages in the chat to free up room.
Upgrade her plan to raise the length of a single chat.
questions.explanation: A length limit is reached when one conversation fills the context window. It is separate from the usage limit, and the fix is to start a new chat.
whyWrong: Session resets address the usage limit, which she has barely touched.
Deleting messages is not how the length limit is resolved; a fresh conversation is.
A plan upgrade is a usage decision and does not resolve a full conversation.

questions.stem: A consultant on a paid plan, working in a chat inside Project B, asks Claude to find a pricing discussion she had inside Project A. Claude cannot find it. What should she do?
options: Turn off memory so chat search can reach every project.
Ask Claude to search again using the client's full name.
Search from inside Project A, where those chats are reachable.
Run the request in an incognito chat to widen the search.
questions.explanation: Chat search covers chats outside projects or within a single project, but not across projects. She needs to search from inside the project that holds the discussion.
whyWrong: Turning off memory does not change that chat search stays within one project.
A different search term does not help when the chats are outside the searchable scope.
Incognito chats are never searched, so this would not widen anything.

questions.stem: A procurement team plans to use Claude to screen incoming vendor requests. Before they build the workflow or tune any instructions, what should they settle first?
options: Polished instructions that cover every request type the team expects
A shared project name that describes the screening goal
A definition of success and a way to test it
A date on which the team will stop reviewing outputs
questions.explanation: Without a clear picture of a good result and a way to check it, the team cannot tell whether any change to the workflow helps.
whyWrong: Instructions written before success is defined cannot be judged, so polishing them first is premature.
A project name is only for organizing and does not define or test quality.
Dropping review by a set date skips the evidence the team needs to judge the workflow.

questions.stem: An analyst must brief executives tomorrow from a requirements document in Word. File creation is enabled on her plan, and the deck goes straight to senior leaders. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Upload the document and review the deck Claude builds
Upload the document and send Claude's deck out unchecked
Retype the key points into slides by hand tonight
Ask IT to build a connector that reads Word files
questions.explanation: With file creation on, Claude can convert a Word document into a presentation, and she should still review the deck before executives see it.
whyWrong: Claude's output can contain errors, so a deck for senior leaders needs a human read-through first.
Claude can convert between file types when file creation is on, so retyping is unnecessary work.
A custom connector is technical work for reaching external systems, and an uploaded file needs none.

questions.stem: A strategist runs Research from her phone, expecting it to use the company's connected Drive as well as the web. The report cites only public web pages. What should she do?
options: Ask IT to reconnect Drive in organization settings
Accept the report as complete and move on
Install a local server in Claude Desktop and rerun on her phone
Rerun the request on the web or in Desktop
questions.explanation: In the mobile app, Research searches only the web and silently skips connectors. Starting it on the web or in Desktop includes internal sources.
whyWrong: Nothing suggests the connector was revoked; the same connector works when Research starts on web or Desktop.
The report is missing the Drive sources she needed, so accepting it leaves a known gap.
Research cannot use tools from local servers in Desktop, so installing one would not help.

questions.stem: A consultant on a Pro plan plans ten Research reports today for a Friday client deadline, and needs her allowance to last the whole week. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Budget each report as if it were a short chat
Expect heavy usage and watch Settings > Usage
Run all ten now and adjust only if a limit appears
Ask Claude in chat how many reports her plan allows
questions.explanation: Research pulls many sources and can use limits faster than normal chat. Settings > Usage shows session and weekly limits so she can judge whether her plan fits.
whyWrong: Research uses limits faster than chat because it retrieves many sources, so this plan would run short.
Waiting for a limit to appear risks losing the rest of the week's allowance before the deadline.
Claude does not reliably know her plan's remaining allowance; Settings > Usage shows it.

questions.stem: A finance lead wants Claude to apply the team's monthly variance-commentary format every time, so she builds a skill. Which TWO practices help the skill work well? (Choose two.)
options: Write a specific description saying when the skill applies
Combine commentary, budgeting and travel policy in one skill
Keep the description vague so it triggers in any chat
Test it with several different prompts after uploading
Skip testing once the skill has been uploaded
questions.explanation: A specific description tells Claude when to use the skill, and trying it with varied prompts after upload shows whether it behaves as intended.
whyWrong: Each skill should have one purpose, so separate tasks belong in separate skills.
A vague description makes it unclear when Claude should use the skill.
Uploading does not prove the skill works; testing with varied prompts is how you find out.

questions.stem: A manager names a project "Contract reviews: always flag auto-renewal clauses" and expects Claude to follow it, but Claude ignores the rule. How should she fix the design?
options: Rename the project in capital letters so the rule stands out
Archive and unarchive the project so Claude refreshes its settings
Move the rule into the project's instructions field
Add the rule to the project description field
questions.explanation: Claude cannot see a project's name or description. Anything it should follow belongs in the instructions or knowledge.
whyWrong: Formatting changes do nothing, because Claude never sees the project name at all.
Archiving keeps everything as it is and does not make Claude read the name.
The description is also hidden from Claude, so it fails for the same reason as the name.

questions.stem: A sales operations lead wants Claude to read the company's internal quoting database through a custom connector. No server for it exists yet. Who should do what?
options: Paste the schema into connector settings so Claude builds a server
Ask IT to build and host the remote server
Ask Claude in chat to host the server for her
Upload a database export to a project and call it a connector
questions.explanation: Building and hosting a remote MCP server is technical work for IT. Once it exists, it is added as a connector.
whyWrong: Connector settings only register an existing server; they do not generate one from a schema.
Claude does not host servers for users, and the server must be provided by the organization.
A project holding an uploaded export is static knowledge, not a live connector.

questions.stem: A support agent's company ticketing connector fails every time with an error that Claude cannot reach its server. IT built it last week, and she cannot change network settings. What should she do first?
options: Reinstall Claude Desktop and add the connector again herself
Work around it by pasting ticket data into chat
Keep retrying the connector until it eventually works
Report the failure and the error message to IT
questions.explanation: A company connector is built and run by IT, and one on a private network can fail if Anthropic is not allowed through the firewall. She should report the problem and the error to IT rather than try to fix servers or networks herself.
whyWrong: Reinstalling Claude does not fix a problem on the company's server or network side.
The workaround leaves the broken connector unreported, so it stays broken for the whole team.
Repeated retries do not change a server or network problem that only IT can diagnose.

questions.stem: A Team plan owner is rolling out file creation to the finance group, whose files hold sensitive figures. Which TWO steps fit sound rollout practice? (Choose two.)
options: Allow every domain from day one so nothing is blocked
Confirm file creation is turned on in the organization's settings
Let staff send generated files out without a review step
Skip guidance and let staff discover the limits on their own
Start with network access off and add only vetted domains
questions.explanation: Owners decide whether file creation is enabled, and the safer approach is to start with network access off and add only vetted domains as needed.
whyWrong: Allowing all domains is the riskiest setting and should not be the starting point.
Generated files can contain mistakes, so they need a human review before they go out.
Staff need guidance on sensible use and limits before relying on file creation.

questions.stem: A director asks you to promise that the team can have Claude build many reports and decks every day from uploaded files. What is the accurate message to give her?
options: File work has caps and uses limits faster than chat
Nothing limits file work, so the team can generate freely
File work counts against usage just as chat does
Caps apply to uploads only, so downloads have no limit
questions.explanation: File creation has a 30MB per-file limit for uploads and downloads and consumes more of the plan's usage than ordinary chat, so volume should be sized accordingly.
whyWrong: File work runs under the same plan usage limits and consumes more of them than normal chat.
File work consumes more of the usage limit than ordinary chat, so the usage point is wrong.
The 30MB maximum applies to downloads as well as uploads.

questions.stem: A project lead tells her team that Research will use a tool running on her own computer and connected to Claude Desktop. A colleague knows this is wrong. What should the colleague correct?
options: Research reaches tools on her computer only in the mobile app
Research reaches tools on her computer only on Team plans
Research cannot use tools that run on her own computer
Research uses those tools but asks approval for each call
questions.explanation: Research cannot use tools from local servers (MCP servers on the user's own computer) configured in Claude Desktop, so that expectation should be set before the team relies on it.
whyWrong: Mobile Research searches only the web and skips connectors, so it cannot reach tools on her computer either.
Plan type does not change this limitation, which applies to tools on her computer connected to Desktop.
Research cannot use these tools at all, and its connector calls for other tools may run without approval.

questions.stem: An operations analyst has a folder of 60 receipts on her laptop and must produce an expense report with working formulas. She is on a paid plan. Which approach best fits this multi-step file task?
options: Paste each receipt's text into separate chats and merge the totals by hand.
Describe the receipts in one chat message and ask for a finished report.
Use Cowork in the desktop app so Claude works through the folder.
Upload one receipt at a time and track the running total yourself.
questions.explanation: Cowork is built for multi-step file tasks that Claude plans and carries out, and the desktop app is what gives it access to local files. It is available on paid plans.
whyWrong: This does the combining work by hand and wastes the point of delegating.
Claude cannot see files that were only described to it, so the report would be guesswork.
This turns a multi-step job into manual bookkeeping and gains little.

questions.stem: A department head will brief her team before a Cowork pilot. Everyone is on a paid plan. Which message about Cowork's value and limits is the most accurate?
options: It handles multi-step file tasks but uses more usage than quick questions.
It answers every question faster than chat and costs the same usage.
It runs on every plan, including Free, and skips approval prompts.
It produces finished files that need no human review before use.
questions.explanation: Cowork suits multi-step file and research work, and because each step consumes tokens, such tasks use more of your usage than quick questions.
whyWrong: Multi-step tasks use more usage than a quick chat answer, not the same.
Cowork is for paid plans only, and approval modes still exist.
Outputs still need review, especially when the work has real consequences.

questions.stem: A requirements analyst receives vendor specification PDFs containing pricing tables and must compare them in a spreadsheet by Friday. File creation is enabled. What is the most appropriate way to use Claude?
options: Retype the tables by hand and ask Claude only to proofread the sheet.
Ask Claude to recall each vendor's typical pricing from general knowledge.
Ask Claude to summarize the PDFs and paste the summaries into cells.
Have Claude pull the tables into Excel, then spot-check the figures.
questions.explanation: Extracting PDF tables into a spreadsheet is a task Claude can do with file creation, and the analyst should still review the result against the sources.
whyWrong: This keeps the slow manual step and delegates only the minor one.
General knowledge would not reflect these vendors' actual quoted prices.
Summaries lose the exact figures that the comparison depends on.

questions.stem: A consultant drafted a project proposal as a document artifact in Claude. The client requires the final version as a Word file. What should she do?
options: Retype the proposal into Word and reapply the formatting by hand.
Export the document artifact directly to Word.
Ask the client to open the artifact link in a browser.
Screenshot each page and send the images as the final file.
questions.explanation: Document artifacts can be exported in standard formats, including Word, PDF, Markdown and Google Docs.
whyWrong: This repeats work that a direct export already does.
The client asked for a Word file, not a link.
Images of pages cannot be edited, so they do not meet the requirement.

questions.stem: A coordinator uploaded a skill for weekly status reports, but Claude seldom uses it. Its description reads only "Helps with documents." What is the best next step?
options: Add several unrelated tasks to the skill so it triggers more often.
Rename the skill and upload it again without changing anything else.
Tell Claude at the start of every chat to ignore other skills.
Rewrite the description to say exactly what the skill does and when.
questions.explanation: A specific description tells Claude when to invoke a skill, so a vague one is the likely cause. After editing, test it with varied prompts.
whyWrong: Skills work best with one purpose, and extra tasks make the match vaguer.
A new name does not tell Claude when the skill applies.
This is a workaround repeated every chat and does not fix the skill.

questions.stem: A manager finished a quarterly project and wants it out of her project list, but she may need its shared knowledge next quarter. What should she do?
options: Delete the project and upload the same files again next quarter.
Rename the project so Claude stops using its knowledge files.
Archive the project, which keeps its sharing settings and knowledge.
Remove all members and files first, then archive the project.
questions.explanation: Archiving tidies the list while preserving members, permission levels and project knowledge, and unarchiving restores everything as it was.
whyWrong: Deleting discards the knowledge and sharing setup she wants to keep.
Claude cannot see a project's name, so renaming does nothing to its files.
Stripping members and files destroys the setup that archiving would preserve.

questions.stem: A planner asks Claude about the same 80-page policy handbook dozens of times a week and keeps hitting her usage limits. What process change helps most?
options: Attach the handbook again in every new chat to keep it fresh.
Upload the handbook once to a project and ask questions there.
Split the handbook into pages and send each page separately.
Turn on Research so Claude pulls the handbook sections itself.
questions.explanation: Reused reference material belongs in a project, where cached portions count less against limits than new content sent each time.
whyWrong: Re-sending the full file each chat counts it in full every time.
Sending pages separately adds messages and repeats the same content.
Research tends to use limits faster because it pulls from many sources.

questions.stem: A strategist tells leadership that Research gives deeper answers than normal chat. Leadership asks what to expect about limits. Which statement is the most accurate?
options: Research uses about the same amount of usage as a short chat.
Research always includes connected tools, whichever device you start it on.
Research works on the Free plan with no extra setup required.
Research searches many sources, so sessions can use limits faster.
questions.explanation: Research retrieves multiple sources, so its sessions can use up your limits faster than ordinary conversations.
whyWrong: Pulling many sources makes Research heavier than a short chat.
On mobile, Research skips connectors without any warning.
Research is offered on paid plans, not Free.

questions.stem: A team lead plans a heavy week of Claude work and wants to stretch her team's usage limits. Which TWO planning steps fit? (Choose two.)
options: Group related questions into a single message where possible.
Open a fresh chat and re-explain the context before each follow-up.
Turn on Research for every quick factual lookup to be thorough.
Keep reused reference files in a project, not reattached each time.
Attach the whole document set to every message for safety.
questions.explanation: Batching related requests cuts back-and-forth messages, and keeping reused files in a project means cached content counts less against limits.
whyWrong: Re-explaining context in new chats adds messages and repeated content.
Research uses limits faster, so it suits deep questions, not quick lookups.
Attaching everything each time makes every message heavier.

questions.stem: Before a demo, a manager drafts talking points about Claude's file creation for executives. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: File work costs about the same usage as a short ordinary chat.
Claude can build Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files from your data.
Finished files are ready to send out without any human review.
File tasks can run as long as needed with no time limits.
Outputs may need review and refinement to meet exact requirements.
questions.explanation: File creation produces Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files, but results can need review and refinement, and the work draws more usage than ordinary chat and has duration limits.
whyWrong: File work consumes more usage than ordinary chat.
Outputs may need review and refinement before they are used.
Tasks and sandbox sessions are time-limited.

questions.stem: An analyst spends two days each month turning a sales CSV into a formatted report. File creation is on, and the report goes to executives. What redesign is most appropriate?
options: Send the CSV to executives and let them ask Claude directly.
Keep the manual process and use Claude only to write the cover email.
Have Claude build the report from the CSV, then review it before sending.
Have Claude build the report and send it straight to executives.
questions.explanation: Turning a CSV into a report is a delegable file task, but the analyst stays accountable by reviewing the output before it goes out.
whyWrong: This pushes the analysis onto executives and loses a consistent report.
This leaves the slow step untouched and gives up the main benefit.
Skipping review risks sending errors to executives.
