questions.stem: A Pro-plan analyst must finish an expense report in Cowork, then prepare an unrelated slide deck. She is close to her weekly limit. Which approach best conserves usage?
options: Keep related steps together and start a new conversation for the deck.
Run both jobs in one long session so earlier context carries over to both.
Switch to Auto mode so Claude finishes each step without interruptions.
Split the expense report into many tiny tasks, one for each receipt.
questions.explanation: Cowork guidance is to group related work into one task and start new conversations for unrelated work, since each step in a multi-step task consumes usage.
whyWrong: Carrying unrelated context along makes every step heavier.
Auto mode consumes more of the usage limit than the other modes.
Many small tasks multiply the setup and steps instead of reducing them.

questions.stem: A marketing manager wants Claude to act as a playful copy editor, but only for one campaign's work and not for her everyday chats. Where should she put this direction?
options: Put it in Instructions for Claude in her profile
Retype it at the top of each new campaign chat
Upload it as a file in the campaign's knowledge
Add it to the instructions of a campaign project
questions.explanation: Project instructions apply to every chat in that project and only there, unlike account-wide profile instructions.
whyWrong: Profile instructions apply to all conversations, which is not what she wants.
Retyping works but is repetitive when saved project instructions apply automatically.
Instructions are not only account-wide; projects have their own, and knowledge holds reference documents.

questions.stem: A team lead shares a private project with an auditor who should read its instructions and knowledge and ask questions in it, but not change anything. Which sharing choice fits?
options: Give her Can edit, so she can chat in the project
Give everyone in the organization access to the project
Tell her no sharing role fits her need
Give her Can view, which allows reading and chatting only
questions.explanation: Can view lets a member see instructions and knowledge and chat in the project without editing; Can edit adds the ability to change them.
whyWrong: Chatting does not require edit rights; that role would let the auditor alter instructions and knowledge.
Organization-wide visibility opens the project to everyone in the organization, not just one person.
Two roles exist, and Can view is the read-and-chat option.

questions.stem: A project on a paid plan holds hundreds of pages of policy files named 'final2', 'scan_07' and 'misc', and Claude now retrieves only parts of them per question. Which habit improves the answers?
options: Use clear filenames and name the document you mean
Merge every document into a single unnamed file for the search tool
Delete the oldest chats from the project to speed up searches
Rename the project to describe all its files
questions.explanation: When retrieval is active, Claude finds the relevant parts of project knowledge, so clear filenames and naming the document you mean help it pick the right content.
whyWrong: One unnamed file gives retrieval nothing to distinguish topics by.
Retrieval searches project knowledge, not old chats.
The project name does not control which files are retrieved.

questions.stem: An analyst connects Drive and asks Claude to summarize a report whose key findings sit in embedded charts. The summary misses them. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask the file owner to grant her full edit access
Convert the whole report into a spreadsheet first
Upload the chart images or describe them in chat
Ask Claude to open a newer version of the file
questions.explanation: When Claude reads a Drive file it extracts text only, so images embedded in documents are not processed; providing the charts directly fills the gap.
whyWrong: Access rights are not the issue; Claude reads only text from Drive files.
Converting to a sheet does not make embedded images readable.
File age is not the cause; the limitation applies to embedded images in any document.

questions.stem: A Team plan owner wants staff to let Claude search and read in a connected app, but wants any action that creates or deletes records blocked. What should the owner do?
options: Allow reads and block writes in the tool permissions
Ask each employee not to request any changes or deletions
Disconnect the connector for everyone on the team
Give every employee Can view access on a project
questions.explanation: Owners can set each group of connector actions to always allow, needs approval or blocked, so reads can stay allowed while writes are blocked, and users cannot override this.
whyWrong: Users cannot override owner settings, and a request is not a control.
Permissions are set per group of actions, so blocking all use is unnecessary.
Project roles govern project content, not what a connector's tools can do.

questions.stem: A product manager always writes 'PRD' for product requirements document and wants brief answers in every chat, in or out of projects. Where should she set this?
options: Copy the preference into each project's instructions
Add it to her profile's Instructions for Claude
Build a custom skill that holds the abbreviations
Upload a glossary file to a project's knowledge
questions.explanation: Instructions for Claude apply to all of your conversations, so they suit general preferences and common terms.
whyWrong: Copying into each project is repetitive and still misses chats outside projects.
A skill is a packaged workflow, not the place for simple everyday preferences.
Project knowledge is used only in that project's chats.

questions.stem: In a project, a manager agreed a budget cap with Claude in one chat. A new chat in the same project shows no knowledge of it. How should she keep the decision available going forward?
options: Switch the project to organization-wide visibility for all its chats
Keep chatting until the new chat catches up
Record the decision in a note in project knowledge
Move the earlier chat out of the project
questions.explanation: Chats in a project do not share context unless the information is saved in the project's knowledge base, so recording and maintaining the decision there keeps it available.
whyWrong: Visibility controls who can see the project, not whether chats share context.
Chats do not merge; each starts without the others' content.
Moving a chat does not share its content with other chats.

questions.stem: A colleague emails an updated ZIP of a custom skill that formats the team's reports, and the team lead wants it live today. Which two steps are sensible before enabling it? (Choose two.)
options: Enable it right away and trust the isolation
Review the bundled files, especially scripts and outside network calls
Skip checking the contents of a colleague's skill
Turn it on for the whole team and review later
Confirm the source is trusted before uploading the ZIP
questions.explanation: Skills can carry prompt-injection or data-exfiltration risk, so install them only from trusted sources and review bundled files, even from a colleague, before enabling.
whyWrong: Skills can carry real risk, including prompt injection and data exfiltration.
A colleague's skill still needs its bundled files reviewed.
Reviewing only after problems appear exposes the whole team to the risk first.

questions.stem: A support lead wants every chat about returns to draw on the team's returns policy document without anyone re-attaching it each time. Where should she put the document?
options: Paste its full text into her profile Instructions for Claude.
Attach it again at the start of each new chat.
Add it to the returns project's knowledge.
Summarize it in one line inside the project instructions.
questions.explanation: Project knowledge is used as context in every chat in that project, so the policy is available without re-uploading.
whyWrong: Profile instructions apply to all her conversations and are for general preferences, not a reference document.
Re-attaching each time is the manual step she wants to avoid.
A one-line summary drops the detail Claude needs from the policy.

questions.stem: On a Team plan, a manager shares a project of draft pricing models. Only her five analysts should see it; one must maintain the files, and the other four should only ask questions. What setup fits?
options: Make it public to the whole organization and ask outsiders not to open it.
Make it private and give all five analysts Can edit access.
Make it public and give the maintainer Can edit access.
Make it private; give the maintainer Can edit and the others Can view.
questions.explanation: A private project is visible only to invited members. Can edit lets the maintainer change knowledge, while Can view lets the others read and chat without changing anything.
whyWrong: A public project is open to everyone in the organization, so asking outsiders not to look protects nothing.
Giving all five edit access lets four people change files they should only use.
A public project is visible to the whole organization, which breaks the five-person limit.

questions.stem: A lawyer uploads a 400-page contract PDF to a chat and asks about a risk chart on page 230. Claude answers from the text but ignores the chart. What is the best fix?
options: Upload the same PDF again and repeat the question.
Save the chart pages as a short PDF and upload that.
Ask Claude to look harder at page 230's visuals.
Convert the whole PDF to a Word document and re-upload.
questions.explanation: PDFs of 101 to 1000 pages are read for text only, while PDFs up to 100 pages have text and visuals read. A short PDF of the chart pages lets Claude see the chart.
whyWrong: Re-uploading the same file gives the same text-only reading.
Claude cannot see visuals it is not given, however it is asked.
Word conversion extracts text only and also cannot read embedded images.

questions.stem: A new Team-plan employee tries the Ask Your Org enterprise search project, but it is unusable because setup has not happened. Who must complete the initial setup before anyone else can use it?
options: Each employee, by connecting their own tools one at a time.
An organization Owner, who chooses connectors for documents and chat.
Anthropic support, after receiving a request from the team.
The first employee to open the project, on behalf of everyone.
questions.explanation: An Owner must complete the initial enterprise search setup, including choosing connectors for documents and chat, before other members can use it.
whyWrong: Employees authenticate their own accounts later, but cannot complete the organization's setup.
Setup is done by an Owner within the organization, not by a request to support.
Ordinary members cannot set up enterprise search on behalf of the organization.

questions.stem: A Team-plan sales director uses Ask Your Org to find a pay-grade spreadsheet in a connected Drive. It returns nothing, though a colleague says the file is in a folder she cannot open. Why?
options: Results follow her own permissions in the connected tools.
Spreadsheets are not supported by enterprise search at all.
The index refreshes weekly, so new files appear later.
An Owner must re-run the whole setup before she sees it.
questions.explanation: Enterprise search signs each person in with their own account, so they see only data they have permission to access in the original systems.
whyWrong: Enterprise search covers documents in connected tools; file type is not the reason here.
Timing does not explain it; her access in the source tool does.
Setup is already done; the missing result comes from her access, not the configuration.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst needs a one-off analysis of three 80MB reports and wants the simplest way to give them to Claude. Where should she upload them?
options: Attach them directly to a chat.
Add them to a new project's knowledge.
Compress each report below 30MB before uploading.
Paste each report's text into the chat.
questions.explanation: A chat accepts files up to 500MB each, while project files are limited to 30MB each, so attaching directly to a chat is simplest for a one-off job.
whyWrong: Project files are limited to 30MB each, so 80MB reports would not fit.
Compressing is extra work that a chat's higher limit makes unnecessary.
Pasting long reports as text is slow and can lose layout and tables.

questions.stem: A communications director's project instructions say only 'Be professional,' and replies vary widely in tone and length. How should she rewrite the instructions?
options: Repeat 'Be professional' in capitals several times.
Add a long list of banned words and phrases.
State the audience, tone and format, and why each matters.
Replace them with a single word that names the desired tone.
questions.explanation: Effective instructions are specific about what is wanted and explain the purpose or audience, so Claude can tailor replies to the goal rather than follow a bare rule.
whyWrong: Capitals and repetition add emphasis, not the detail that is missing.
A list of things to avoid tells Claude what not to do instead of what to produce.
One word is even less specific than the current instruction.

questions.stem: A product manager works in many projects and in plain chats. Which two preferences belong in her account-wide Instructions for Claude rather than one project's instructions? (Choose two.)
options: Lead every answer with the conclusion, then the supporting detail.
Treat uploaded files as one client account's contracts.
Write dates as day, month, year in every reply.
Follow the brand voice guide for the spring launch.
Cite section numbers from the launch handbook in answers.
questions.explanation: Account-wide Instructions for Claude apply to all conversations, so they suit general preferences. Details tied to one account, launch or handbook belong in that project's instructions.
whyWrong: This describes files for one account, so it belongs in that account's project.
A brand voice guide for one launch is project-specific context.
Handbook section numbers apply only where the handbook is used, so a project fits better.

questions.stem: A travel policy changed, and a team's project still holds last year's version in its knowledge. Which two actions keep the project reliable? (Choose two.)
options: Keep both versions and remind Claude in each chat which is current.
Remove last year's policy file from the project's knowledge.
Attach the new policy only inside one chat.
Rename the old file 'misc' so it ranks lower.
Upload the new policy with a clear, descriptive filename.
questions.explanation: Removing the outdated file and adding the new one with a descriptive name keeps the project's shared knowledge current. Content can be added or removed at any time.
whyWrong: Keeping both versions relies on reminders in every chat and invites mix-ups.
A file attached in one chat is not shared with the project's other chats.
A vague name makes the old file harder to identify and does not remove it.

questions.stem: A project manager connected Drive for a client engagement that has now ended, but she still has chats in progress on other work. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave it connected and ignore it in future prompts.
Delete the finished engagement's chats from her history.
Ask Claude in each chat to avoid using Drive files.
Disconnect the Drive connector in her connector settings.
questions.explanation: Services that are no longer needed should be disconnected in the connector settings, which keeps access limited to what the work requires.
whyWrong: Leaving it connected keeps access open that she no longer needs.
Deleting chats does not remove the connection to Drive.
A per-chat request does not remove the connection and is easy to forget.

questions.stem: An HR team wants Claude to rank applicants and have a coordinator send rejections straight from the ranking with no review. Under Anthropic's Usage Policy, which concern is correct?
options: Employment is not a covered area, so no safeguards apply
Employment is high-risk, so a qualified person reviews first
Only the applicant's consent is required before rankings are used
Review is needed only for approvals, never for rejections
questions.explanation: Employment is a high-risk area, so a qualified person with authority to change the recommendation must review it before it drives a decision.
whyWrong: Employment is listed among the high-risk areas that need extra safeguards.
The policy requires meaningful human review, not just consent from the person affected.
The exception for skipping review covers only recommendations wholly favorable to the person, which rejections are not.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator is weighing four requests for Claude. Which one is off-limits for every user under Anthropic's Usage Policy, whatever review process is in place?
options: Summarize a lease for a tenant, with a paralegal checking it
Draft a product FAQ mentioning insurance, approved by compliance
Summarize benefits rules for a caseworker who verifies each answer
Produce fake customer reviews under invented customer accounts
questions.explanation: Creating deceptive, artificial activity such as fake reviews breaks the universal usage standards, which apply to every user and use. The other tasks touch high-risk areas but are allowed with proper review.
whyWrong: Legal topics are high-risk, but this task is allowed when a qualified person reviews the output.
Insurance is a high-risk area, but a compliance-approved FAQ is permitted with human review.
Public benefits are a high-risk area, and caseworker verification supplies the review needed.

questions.stem: A clinic manager proposes sending Claude's medication advice to patients through a portal. Compliance asks which safeguard fits the policy for medical recommendations. What is the best answer?
options: Have a licensed clinician review and amend each answer
Add a footer saying Claude can make mistakes
Name Claude as the model used with each answer
Have an administrator glance at answers but not alter them
questions.explanation: Medical recommendations are high-risk, so a qualified person must meaningfully review them and have authority to change them before they reach patients.
whyWrong: A warning label is not a review; the recommendation still reaches patients unchecked.
Disclosure matters, but telling patients the model name does not replace review before delivery.
A reviewer with no authority to modify the advice does not meet the human-in-the-loop requirement.

questions.stem: A freelancer on a Pro plan pastes confidential client drafts into Claude and worries that her chats could be used for model training. Which statement is accurate?
options: Anthropic sets training use for every Pro account
Only Team and Enterprise users can decide this setting
She decides, and can change it, in Privacy Settings
Her choice is locked after she signs up
questions.explanation: On Free, Pro and Max plans the user decides whether chats and coding sessions are used for training, and can change the choice at any time in Privacy Settings.
whyWrong: Consumer plans give the user control over this setting.
Team and Enterprise fall under commercial terms, where this consumer choice does not apply.
The setting can be changed at any time, not just once.

questions.stem: A Max plan user handling confidential client notes is deciding whether to let her chats be used for training. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Declining training deletes all her data immediately
The setting also governs any Team workspace she belongs to
Allowing training means her chats are kept much longer
Her choice applies to every earlier idle chat as well
Declining training leaves the shorter standard retention in place
questions.explanation: Allowing training extends how long her chats are kept, while declining leaves the standard, shorter retention period in place. The choice is hers and is not tied to any Team plan.
whyWrong: Declining does not delete data at once; the standard retention period continues.
Team plans fall under commercial terms, so the consumer choice does not apply to them.
The change applies to new or resumed chats, and earlier idle chats are not used for training.

questions.stem: A user typed her project budget into a chat, then deleted the conversation. Claude still mentions the budget in new chats. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait up to 30 days for the deletion to apply
Delete that entry in Settings > Memory
Reset all memory to clear every saved entry
Open an incognito chat to erase stored memories
questions.explanation: Deleting a conversation does not remove memories generated from it. Each memory entry can be deleted individually in Settings > Memory.
whyWrong: There is no delay mechanism; the memory entry simply persists on its own.
Individual entries can be deleted, so wiping every memory with a reset is unnecessary.
Incognito chats are not saved to memory going forward but cannot erase memories already stored.

questions.stem: A teammate finds a custom connector from an unknown developer that promises automatic CRM cleanup, and wants it added to the team's setup. Which action fits sound governance?
options: Confirm the server is trusted and review its scopes first
Add it now and rely on Anthropic's verification
Add it with full scopes and narrow them later
Add it for Research only, where every call needs approval
questions.explanation: Anthropic does not verify custom connectors, so only trusted servers should be connected, with requested permissions reviewed and scopes limited.
whyWrong: Custom connectors are not verified by Anthropic, so trust is the team's responsibility.
Granting full scopes first exposes data; scopes should be limited from the start.
Research can call connector tools automatically without approval, so it is riskier, not safer.

questions.stem: A manager shares a project with "Can view" access with outside contractors. Its knowledge includes a salary spreadsheet, and she assumes view-only hides the file. What is the most accurate statement?
options: View-only members see the instructions but never the uploaded files
Only members' own chats are visible, so the spreadsheet stays private
Knowledge is visible only to members with Can edit
Both roles see knowledge, so keep sensitive files out
questions.explanation: Sharing a project gives members its knowledge and instructions at either permission level, so sensitive files should not be in a shared project.
whyWrong: Knowledge and instructions are both visible to view-only members.
Chats stay unshared, but that does not protect files that are part of the project knowledge.
Both permission levels can see the knowledge; edit rights only add the ability to change things.

questions.stem: A benefits office uses Claude to draft eligibility explanations that staff review before sending to applicants. Counsel asks what the policy says about telling applicants. What is the best answer?
options: Name Claude and the exact model version in each letter
Skip disclosure once a staff member approves each letter
Tell applicants that AI was used, without naming Claude
Tell only internal staff about the AI use
questions.explanation: People affected by advice or decisions produced with AI must be clearly told AI was used, though naming Claude or the model is not required.
whyWrong: Naming Claude or the model is not required, so this overstates the rule.
Human review and disclosure are separate requirements, and review does not replace telling applicants.
The duty to disclose runs to the people affected, not just to internal staff.

questions.stem: An analyst will run Research with a custom ticketing connector that has tools to read tickets and tools to update them. Which TWO precautions are sensible? (Choose two.)
options: Assume Research asks before every connector call
Disable connector tools that write or change data
Skip reviewing tool inputs and outputs entirely
Review every approval request before allowing it
Grant broad scopes so Research is never interrupted
questions.explanation: Research can call connector tools automatically without approval, so write-capable tools should be disabled and approval requests reviewed carefully, given the risk of hidden instructions from a bad server.
whyWrong: Research can invoke connector tools without asking, so doing nothing leaves write actions exposed.
Claude has protections, but tool inputs and outputs should still be reviewed for hidden instructions.
Limiting scopes reduces harm if something goes wrong, so broad scopes work against that.

questions.stem: A coworker publishes an artifact budgeting tool for the whole team and asks everyone to enter their own salary details. Before typing anything sensitive, what should you check?
options: Check whether it uses storage everyone can see
Check whether its title matches the budgeting project
Check whether it was exported to PDF first
Check whether memory is paused for artifacts
questions.explanation: The builder decides what is personal and what is shared, so sensitive data should be entered only after confirming the artifact does not use shared storage.
whyWrong: A title says nothing about where entered data is stored or who can see it.
Export format does not reveal how an artifact stores or shares data.
Pausing memory does not control the artifact's own storage, which is where the exposure lies.

questions.stem: A sales rep on a Pro plan wants to show a customer a Claude chat that includes internal margin figures. She is considering a public link. What should she understand first?
options: Viewers must sign in to Claude, which limits who can open it.
Anyone with the link can view it, so treat it as public.
Turning the link off later also deletes copies others made.
Only the final message is visible, so the margins stay hidden.
questions.explanation: No account is needed to open a public link, so anyone who gets it can read the chat, and anyone can copy or screenshot it. Do not share content you would not post openly.
whyWrong: No Claude account is required to view a public link.
Turning a link off stops it working but cannot remove copies already made.
A shared snapshot includes all messages sent before sharing, not just the last.

questions.stem: A manager shared a chat on Monday, then kept adding messages and attached a spreadsheet. On Tuesday, what can her colleague see through the shared link?
options: The full conversation, including the new messages and the attached spreadsheet.
All the new messages, but not the attached spreadsheet.
Nothing; the link stops working once she keeps chatting.
Only messages sent before sharing; the spreadsheet stays private.
questions.explanation: A shared chat is a snapshot of the messages sent before sharing. Later messages stay private unless she unshares and shares again, and attached files are not included.
whyWrong: Sharing is a frozen snapshot, so later messages are not added.
Later messages are not added to the snapshot either.
The snapshot link keeps working; it does not update or expire when she chats.

questions.stem: A consultant needs to show one client contact a chat containing the client's project details. Which sharing method fits best?
options: Invite the contact's email address to view a snapshot of the chat.
Create a public link and send it only to the contact.
Copy the conversation into an email and attach the original files.
Screenshot the chat and post it in a shared team channel.
questions.explanation: Sharing with specific people keeps the chat private to the invited address and gives view-only access to a snapshot.
whyWrong: Anyone who obtains a public link can read it, so it is not limited to one person.
This spreads the details beyond the chosen contact and shares files unnecessarily.
A team channel exposes the client's details to people who do not need them.

questions.stem: A Team plan employee cannot find any option to create a public link for a chat she wants to share outside the company. What explains this?
options: Public links need a personal Pro upgrade for each Team member.
Public links appear only after Anthropic reviews the chat's content.
Team chats can be shared only inside the same organization.
Admins must approve public links for each individual shared chat.
questions.explanation: On Team and Enterprise, sharing stays inside the organization and public links are not available. Admins can also turn sharing off, review shared chats and revoke them.
whyWrong: Plan upgrades do not change the organization-only rule for Team chats.
There is no content review step that unlocks public links.
Admins can turn sharing off or revoke chats, but there is no per-chat approval for public links.

questions.stem: An analyst plans to open a spreadsheet from an unknown sender with file creation on. Her project holds confidential client contracts. What is the most prudent step?
options: Upload it to the project and ask Claude to scan it for hidden instructions.
Handle it in a separate chat outside the confidential project.
Upload it to the project and rely on Claude's built-in protections.
Delete the sender's name from the file, then add it to the project.
questions.explanation: External files can carry hidden instructions, and Claude can only expose data it can reach through the prompt, project or connections. Keeping the file away from the contracts limits that exposure.
whyWrong: Asking Claude to check its own input is not a reliable safeguard.
Built-in protections reduce the risk but do not remove it, and the contracts stay within reach.
Removing a name does not make the file's contents safe.

questions.stem: An employee wants to ask Claude about a sensitive personal health matter without it affecting memory or later chat searches. What is the best approach?
options: Ask in a project chat, then delete the conversation afterward.
Ask in a regular chat, then reset memory when finished.
Turn on the opt-in setting that stores sensitive topics first.
Start an incognito chat outside any project.
questions.explanation: Incognito chats are not saved to memory or chat history, and Claude does not pull from them when searching past conversations.
whyWrong: Deleting a conversation does not remove memories generated from it.
Resetting permanently erases all memories, which is far broader than needed.
That setting makes Claude more willing to store sensitive topics, the opposite of the goal.

questions.stem: A team member is tidying her Claude memory settings before a sensitive client project starts. Which TWO statements about the controls are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Deleting a conversation also removes every memory generated from it.
Pausing memory keeps stored memories but stops using and adding them.
Resetting memory can be reversed by turning memory back on.
Resetting memory permanently deletes all memories, including project memories.
Incognito chats still add to memory but not to chat history.
questions.explanation: Pausing keeps memories but Claude neither uses them nor adds new ones, while resetting permanently deletes everything, project memories included.
whyWrong: Memories from a deleted conversation must be deleted individually in memory settings.
A reset cannot be undone; she would start from scratch.
Incognito chats do not contribute to memory at all.

questions.stem: An analyst wants Skip mode in Cowork for a task that edits files other teams rely on. Which statement about the approval modes is accurate?
options: Skip still runs a safety check on every action, as Auto does.
Skip still asks before each action, as Manual mode does.
Skip performs no automatic checks, so trust everything involved first.
Skip uses the most usage of the three modes.
questions.explanation: Skip does not pause to ask and nothing checks actions automatically, so it suits only work where you completely trust every action, connector and file. Consequential work calls for Manual.
whyWrong: Automatic safety checks belong to Auto mode, not Skip.
Asking for permission on each action is what Manual mode does.
It is Auto mode that uses more of the usage limit, and Skip has no checks.

questions.stem: A claims team has Claude propose outcomes. Claims paid in full go out automatically; partial approvals and denials go to a qualified adjuster who can change them. What is the best assessment?
options: Sound; only fully favorable decisions may skip review, where law allows.
Unsound; every claim outcome needs a qualified person's review first.
Unsound; Claude may not be used for any insurance decision.
Sound; partial approvals may also skip review when amounts are small.
questions.explanation: Insurance claims are a high-risk area. Wholly favorable decisions may skip human review where the law permits, but partial approvals and denials need meaningful review by a qualified person who can change the outcome.
whyWrong: Wholly favorable decisions are the one exempted case, where law permits.
Insurance is permitted with safeguards; it is not banned outright.
Partial approvals or conditional approvals do not qualify for the exemption.

questions.stem: A shop owner asks Claude to write fifty glowing customer reviews under invented names for her product page. What is the appropriate response?
options: Write them, and add a note that the reviews are AI-generated.
Write them if the owner confirms the products are genuinely good.
Write them if a manager reviews each one before publishing.
Decline; fake reviews are prohibited for all users.
questions.explanation: Fake reviews are a deceptive-campaign misuse covered by the universal usage standards, which apply to every user whatever review or disclosure is added.
whyWrong: Disclosure does not make invented customer reviews acceptable.
The quality of the product does not change that the reviewers are fabricated.
Human review is a safeguard for high-risk areas, not a fix for prohibited uses.

questions.stem: A university plans to use Claude to propose exam grades that decide whether students pass. Which TWO safeguards fit Anthropic's Usage Policy? (Choose two.)
options: Let Claude finalize grades whenever it reports high confidence.
Have a qualified instructor review each grade and change it if needed.
Review only a random sample of grades at the end of each term.
Name the exact Claude model and version on every grade report.
Tell students clearly that AI was used to produce their grades.
questions.explanation: Grading that affects outcomes is a high-risk area. It needs meaningful review by a qualified person with authority to change the result, and clear disclosure that AI was used, though naming Claude is not required.
whyWrong: Claude's own confidence report is not a substitute for qualified human review.
Sampling leaves most grades without meaningful review before they take effect.
Naming the model is not required; the duty is to tell people AI was used.

questions.stem: A sales manager asks Claude to 'improve our onboarding process' and gets a generic list. She wants advice that fits her team. Which change is most likely to give a more useful answer?
options: Ask the same question again and hope for a more specific list.
Add background about the team and split the task into steps.
Add the word 'detailed' and keep the short request otherwise unchanged.
Send one much longer prompt covering every onboarding topic without extra background.
questions.explanation: When an answer misses, state the ask simply, supply full background as if Claude has no context, and break a big task into smaller steps.
whyWrong: Repeating a vague request tends to produce another generic answer.
A single word does not add the context Claude is missing.
A bigger request without context is still vague and is harder to answer well.

questions.stem: A trainer asks Claude for a ten-section course outline, but the reply stops after section four. She wants to keep the same outline and style. What is the best way to get the rest?
options: Open a new chat and ask only for sections five to ten.
Wait several hours, then resend the same prompt unchanged.
Ask Claude to shorten the course to four sections.
Send the earlier prompt and Claude's reply, asking it to continue.
questions.explanation: When an answer is cut short, including your earlier prompt and Claude's reply in the follow-up lets it continue from where it left off.
whyWrong: Without the earlier context Claude cannot continue the same outline consistently.
Waiting is not needed, and resending alone does not show Claude what it already wrote.
Shrinking the scope changes the task rather than recovering the missing sections.

questions.stem: Midmorning, a coordinator sees a message that Claude cannot respond because of unexpected capacity constraints. Her own usage is low and she needs the answer before a noon meeting. What should she do?
options: Wait a few minutes, then try the request again.
Shorten the prompt, then resend it immediately to avoid the error.
Upgrade her plan to clear a used-up five-hour limit.
Clear her browser data to fix a login problem.
questions.explanation: This message means system-wide demand is high; it is not an outage, so waiting a few minutes and retrying is the fix.
whyWrong: The message is about overall demand, not the length of her prompt.
A used-up limit shows a different message with a reset time, not this one.
A login problem shows a separate login error, not a capacity notice.

questions.stem: A recruiter's job posting from Claude has the right requirements but reads as stiff. She has spent twenty minutes in this chat refining the content and wants to keep it. What is the best next step?
options: Start a new chat and retype the original request word for word.
Regenerate the reply again and again until a warmer version appears.
Reply in this chat, naming the stiff lines and requesting warmer wording.
Copy the posting into a document and rewrite the stiff parts by hand.
questions.explanation: Replying in the same chat with specific feedback keeps the good content and lets Claude revise only what felt wrong, rather than starting over or relying on luck.
whyWrong: Starting over discards the good content, and the same wording gives a similar result.
Random retries give no direction, so a warmer version is luck rather than a fix.
Claude can revise its own output when you tell it what to change, so a manual rewrite is unnecessary.

questions.stem: On a paid plan, an analyst sees that her five-hour limit is reached and the notice shows a reset time three hours away. A client deliverable is due in one hour. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Create a second account and continue the urgent work there.
Wait three hours for the reset and deliver the work late.
Delete older chats to restore her remaining usage.
Continue the work using usage credits, if they are enabled.
questions.explanation: A limit-reached notice means the five-hour or weekly allowance is used up; with a deadline too close for the reset, a paid plan can continue with usage credits if they are enabled.
whyWrong: Working around limits with extra accounts is not the supported fix.
Waiting misses the deadline, and a paid plan offers a way to continue sooner.
Deleting chats does not give back used allowance.

questions.stem: A team lead sees her team keep hitting its usage limit during routine drafting and document edits. Which two habits would most help stretch usage? (Choose two.)
options: Keep one long chat running for every task.
Start a fresh chat when a long one nears the limit.
Set the highest effort level for every routine task.
Keep every connector and web search on, just in case.
Switch off connectors and web search when not needed.
questions.explanation: Starting a new conversation when a long chat nears the limit, and turning off tools a chat does not need, both reduce how much each message uses.
whyWrong: Long chats use more of the limit with each new message.
Higher effort uses more of the limit and suits hard problems, not routine tasks.
Tools and connectors are token-intensive, so leaving them on without need costs usage.

questions.stem: A team keeps its style guide in a Project. On Monday, after a week away, the first message used much more of their limit than the follow-ups that day. What best explains this?
options: Claude forgot the style guide and the team had to upload it again.
The Project cache expired during inactivity, so files counted in full again.
Follow-up messages cost nothing, and only first messages count toward limits.
Project files count in full on every message, whatever the timing.
questions.explanation: Documents in a Project are cached, so reuse counts less, but the cache expires after inactivity and the first message afterward counts that content in full.
whyWrong: Nothing was re-uploaded; the difference comes from the cache, not forgetting.
Follow-ups are not free; they simply count cached content for less.
Cached Project content counts less on reuse, which is the benefit of Projects.

questions.stem: A user sees 'There was an error logging you in' when opening Claude in a browser. Which set of first steps does Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance suggest?
options: Switch to a lower effort level, then try signing in again.
Turn off the VPN and clear cache, cookies and extensions.
Create a second account and move all the chats over to it.
Wait for the weekly usage limit to reset and try again.
questions.explanation: The help article lists turning off a VPN, disabling browser extensions, and clearing cache and cookies as the first steps for this generic login error.
whyWrong: Effort settings have no bearing on signing in.
A new account does not address the cause and loses history.
This message is not a usage-limit notice.

questions.stem: A legal assistant pastes a very large set of documents and sees 'Your message will exceed the length limit for this chat.' What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait five minutes, then send the very same message again.
Turn on usage credits and then send the message again.
Send the content in smaller parts or fewer files.
Tell Claude to ignore the length limit just this once.
questions.explanation: This error means the input is too large for the chat. Sending smaller parts, attaching fewer files, summarizing, or starting a new conversation resolves it.
whyWrong: The limit concerns message size, not temporary demand.
Credits cover usage limits and do not enlarge the context window.
Claude cannot override the context size of a chat.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst finds Claude's default-effort answers shallow when analyzing a dense 80-page report for a planning decision. Accuracy matters more than speed. What should she adjust?
options: Raise the effort setting for this analysis.
Lower the effort setting to get faster replies.
Turn off the connectors she is not using.
Start a new chat for every question.
questions.explanation: Higher effort applies more reasoning and suits detailed document analysis, at the cost of longer waits and faster use of limits.
whyWrong: Lower effort gives less thorough answers, the opposite of what she needs.
Turning off connectors saves usage and does not deepen analysis.
New chats lose context and do not add reasoning depth.

questions.stem: An operations lead's team uses Claude all day for simple, repetitive reformatting and keeps hitting usage limits. Quality is already fine and speed matters. Which adjustment fits best?
options: Raise effort to maximum so fewer corrections are needed.
Add long background paragraphs to every message.
Use a lower effort level for these routine tasks.
Keep one long chat running for all the reformatting.
questions.explanation: Low or medium effort suits routine tasks, finishes faster, and stretches usage furthest, so it fits simple work whose quality is already acceptable.
whyWrong: Maximum effort is slower and uses limits fastest.
Extra text adds usage without improving routine work.
Long chats consume more usage than fresh ones.

questions.stem: A customer-success rep asked Claude to 'write an apology note' and got a generic message that fits no situation. The note goes out today. What should he try first?
options: Ask Claude to make the generic note a good deal longer.
Rewrite the request with the situation and tone.
Switch to the largest model and repeat the same request.
Send the generic note and add the details afterward.
questions.explanation: A weak answer often reflects missing background. Writing the request as if Claude knows nothing about the situation gives it what it needs.
whyWrong: Length adds words without adding the missing facts.
A bigger model cannot guess facts it was never given.
Sending a generic note risks the customer relationship.

questions.stem: An analyst sends Claude six separate short messages about the same report and is nearing her session limit. Which habit would save the most usage going forward?
options: Paste the full report again into every single message.
Raise the effort level so the answers need fewer follow-ups.
Delete the chat after each question and start over.
Combine the related questions into one planned message.
questions.explanation: Grouping related questions into one message with full context saves usage and avoids extra back-and-forth.
whyWrong: Repeating the report adds usage with each message.
Higher effort uses limits faster.
Restarting loses context and repeats the setup cost.

questions.stem: A team's project chats keep using up their usage limit by midweek, which stalls their work. Which two changes would help most? (Choose two.)
options: Remove project files the team no longer needs.
Add every team document to the project just in case.
Keep project instructions short and focused.
Run all topics in one ever-growing chat.
Leave every connector on for every chat.
questions.explanation: Short, focused instructions and only the files you need keep the context light, which reduces how much each message uses.
whyWrong: Extra files consume more of the context and usage.
Longer chats use more of the limit.
Connectors are token-intensive and add usage when not needed.
